content: Do not take benazepril if you are pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking benazepril, contact your doctor immediately, as this medication can harm the fetus. Benazepril is prescribed to treat high blood pressure, either alone or in combination with other medications. It belongs to a class of drugs called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by reducing certain chemicals that tighten blood vessels, allowing blood to flow more smoothly. Benazepril is available as an oral tablet and is usually taken once or twice daily, with or without food. To ensure consistent use, take it at the same time every day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take benazepril exactly as directed. Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not take it more frequently than instructed. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it. Benazepril helps control high blood pressure but does not cure it. Continue taking it even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking benazepril, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to benazepril or other ACE inhibitors such as captopril, enalapril, fosinopril, lisinopril, moexipril, perindopril, quinapril, ramipril, or trandolapril, or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention diuretics (water pills), lithium, and potassium supplements. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have recently experienced severe diarrhea or vomiting, or if you have a history of heart failure, kidney disease, lupus, scleroderma, or diabetes. Let your doctor know if you plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking benazepril. Be aware that diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration, or excessive sweating can lead to a drop in blood pressure, causing lightheadedness or fainting. Consult your doctor before using salt substitutes containing potassium. If your doctor prescribes a low-salt or low-sodium diet, follow these instructions carefully. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Benazepril may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: cough, headache, dizziness, or drowsiness. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs; hoarseness; difficulty breathing or swallowing; lightheadedness; fainting; rash; yellowing of the skin or eyes; fever, sore throat, chills, or other signs of infection. If you experience any unusual problems while taking this medication, contact your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store benazepril in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of outdated or unneeded medication properly. Consult your pharmacist about proper disposal methods. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the person has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include dizziness and fainting. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your blood pressure should be checked regularly to monitor your response to benazepril. Your doctor may order lab tests to assess your body’s response to the medication. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
